planting.note: Nick or soak seed coats to speed germination and direct-sow in well-drained sandy soil; this species resents root disturbance so transplanting is best avoided.

directions: Sow seed directly where plants are to grow, since this fast-growing shrubby lupine forms a woody base and does not transplant well once established. It thrives in poor, sandy, well-drained soils along coastal dunes and slopes, tolerating salt spray and drought once rooted in. Fragrant yellow, occasionally blue or lilac, pea-like flower spikes appear from late winter into summer, attracting bees and butterflies. Plants are naturally short-lived, often declining after 5-10 years, and can self-sow aggressively in mild coastal climates.

planting.note: Sow or divide in spring or fall; site with care since this species spreads by deep, brittle rhizomes and is very difficult to fully remove once established.

directions: This vigorous Eurasian bellflower produces one-sided racemes of nodding, violet-blue bell-shaped flowers on upright stems from mid to late summer. It spreads readily by rhizomes as well as self-seeding, making it best confined to naturalized areas, tough spots, or containers rather than refined borders. It tolerates poor soil, drought, and partial shade far better than most border campanulas, but gardeners should be prepared for its assertive, colonizing habit. In many regions it has escaped cultivation and is regarded as a persistent garden thug or naturalized weed.
